idiom_name: one method per rule on a parser struct over a go/scanner token stream (go/parser shape)
implementation_notes: Go's own toolchain is the model: go/parser is a hand-written parser whose parser struct embeds a scanner.Scanner and keeps the current token plus position, text/template/parse does the same for a much smaller grammar, and both return errors instead of throwing. In application code a parser is a struct holding the token slice or scanner and an index, one method per rule returning (Node, error), and small helpers (got/want-style) for conditional and required consumption; errors are ordinary positioned values, so callers can collect or abort. What replaces the classic structure is Go's ordinary style rather than a library - no class hierarchy, no exceptions, no tables: the grammar is the set of methods and the error path is the return value. Keep this form for grammars you own, and reuse go/parser when the input is Go source.
pitfalls: Go has no exceptions and no tail-call optimisation: every rule must check and propagate errors, and deep nesting still grows the goroutine stack, so bound recursion depth explicitly for untrusted input.
Slicing tokens loses the base offset; keep the absolute token index and each token's own Pos for diagnostics instead of computing positions from the current slice.
Folding the lexer into the parser (as go/parser embeds its scanner) couples the two; for a custom grammar write a separate tokenizer so rule methods can be tested on token fixtures.
